0.0.n: This greeting is used when answering a phone or checking whether someone can hear you.

0.2.n: The topic marker は is omitted here in casual speech.

0.3.n: 夏 is part of the name 夏芽, not a separate word meaning summer here.

0.4.n: 芽 completes the name 夏芽; do not translate it separately as bud here.

1.0.n: This time word sets the timing for the whole sentence without needing a particle.

1.2.n: 火星 is the Japanese name of the planet Mars.

1.3.n: に marks the location where someone is when used with いる.

1.4.n: いる is the plain form used for the presence of people and animals; the subject I is understood.

1.5.n: Sentence-final の adds an explanatory tone; in statements, this usage often sounds feminine.

2.0.n: This greeting is used when answering a phone or checking whether someone can hear you.

2.2.n: The topic marker は is omitted here in casual speech.

2.3.n: 夏 is part of the name 夏芽, not a separate word meaning summer here.

2.4.n: 芽 completes the name 夏芽; do not translate it separately as bud here.

3.0.n: This time word sets the timing and is immediately repeated.

3.2.n: いま is the hiragana spelling of 今; the following 〜 shows that the sound is drawn out.

3.5.n: 日本 is the country's name, followed by に to mark the speaker's location.

3.6.n: に marks the location where someone is when used with いる.

3.7.n: いる is the plain form used for the presence of people and animals; the subject I is understood.

3.8.n: Sentence-final の adds an explanatory tone; in statements, this usage often sounds feminine.

0.tip: 夏芽 is one name, Natsume, even though the app splits it into two characters.

1.lit: Now, [I] on Mars am, you see.
1.tip: Place + にいる tells where someone is; Japanese often leaves out the subject when it is clear.

2.tip: 夏芽 is one name, Natsume, even though the app splits it into two characters.

3.lit: Now, now..., [I] in Japan am, you see.
3.tip: 今 and いま are the same word; the repetition and drawn-out sound reflect the speaker's delivery.
